title: Why believe Herodotus and not the disciples?
source_text: Λεκτέον δὴ πρὸς τὴν περὶ τοῦ Ἀριστέου ἱστορίαν ὅτι, εἰ μὲν ὁ Κέλσος ὡς ἱστορίαν αὐτὴν ἐξετίθετο, μὴ καὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ συγκατάθεσιν ἐμφαίνων παραδεξαμένου αὐτὴν ὡς ἀληθῆ, αλλως ἂν πρὸς τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ ἀπηντήσαμεν· ἐπεὶ δὲ δαιμονίως αὐτὸν ἠφανίσθαι ἐναργῶς δ᾿ αὖθις φανῆναι καὶ πολλαχοῦ τῆς οἰκουμένης ἐπιδεδημηκέναι φησὶ καὶ θαυμαστὰ ἠγγελκέναι, ἔτι δὲ καὶ χρησμὸν τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος, ἐπισκήψαντος Μεταποντίνοις ἐν θεῶν μοίρᾳ νέμειν τὸν Ἀριστέαν, ὡς ἀφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ καὶ συγκατατιθέμενος ἐκτίθεται, † λόγον τὸν πρὸς αὐτόν· καὶ πῶς ὅλως τε πλάσματα ὑπολαμβάνων τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν Ἰησοῦ μαθητῶν παράδοξα περὶ αὐτοῦ ἀναγεγραμμένα καὶ μεμφόμενος τοῖς πιστεύουσιν αὐτοῖς, ταῦτα οὔ (τε) τερατείαν οὔτε πλάσματα εἶναι νομίζεις; πῶς δὲ καὶ ὁ ἄλλοις ἐγκαλῶν ὡς ἀλόγως πιστεύουσι τοῖς περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ παραδόξοις σὺ τοσούτοις ἐμφαίνῃ πεπιστευκέναι. οὐδεμίαν ἀπόδειξιν περὶ αὐτῶν ἢ κατασκευὴν περὶ τοῦ αὐτὰ γεγονέναι φέρων; ἢ Ἡρόδοτος μὲν καὶ Πίνδαρος ἀψευδεῖν παρὰ σοὶ νομίζονται, οἱ δ᾿ ἀποθνῄσκειν μελετήσαντες ὑπὲρ τῶν Ἰησοῦ μαθημάτων καὶ τοιαῦτα περὶ ὧν ἐπείσθησαν τοῖς ἑξῆς καταλιπόντες γράμματα, περὶ πλασμάτων, ὡς οἴει, καὶ μύθων καὶ τερατειῶν τοσοῦτον ἀγωνίζονται, ὡς καὶ ζῆν περιστατικῶς δι᾿ αὐτὰ καὶ ἀποθνῄσκειν βιαίως; μέσον τοίνυν σαυτὸν στήσας τῶν τε περὶ τοῦ Ἀριστέου γεγραμμένων καὶ τῶν περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἱστορουμένων, ἴδε εἰ μὴ ἐκ τοῦ ἀποβάντος καὶ τῶν ὠφελουμένων εἰς ἠθῶν ἐπανόρθωσιν καὶ εὐλάβειαν τὴν πρὸς τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν ἔστιν εἰπεῖν ὅτι πιστευτέον μὲν ὡς οὐκ ἀθεεὶ γενομένοις τοῖς περὶ Ἰησοῦ ἱστορουμένοις οὐχὶ δὲ τοῖς περὶ τοῦ Προκοννησίου Ἀριστέου.
pass_a_gloss: It must be said (λεκτέον) to the story (ἱστορία) about Aristeas that, if Celsus set it out (ἐκτίθημι) as a story, not also displaying (ἐμφαίνω) his own assent (συγκατάθεσις) as having received (παραδέχομαι) it as true, we would have answered (ἀπαντάω) his argument (λόγος) otherwise; but since he says that he vanished supernaturally (δαιμονίως ἀφανίζω) and clearly appeared again and visited many places of the world and reported wonders, and further also the oracle (χρησμός) of Apollo enjoining (ἐπισκήπτω) the Metapontines to assign Aristeas in the portion of the gods, he sets out as from himself (ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ) and assenting (συγκατατίθεμαι), † [we direct] the argument to him: and how, supposing (ὑπολαμβάνω) wholly (ὅλως) to be fictions (πλάσματα) the marvels about him recorded (ἀναγράφω) by the disciples of Jesus, and blaming (μέμφομαι) those believing them, do you consider these to be neither wonder-mongering (τερατεία) nor fictions? And how do you, who accuse (ἐγκαλέω) others as believing irrationally (ἀλόγως) the marvels about Jesus, appear (ἐμφαίνομαι) to have believed so many things, bringing no demonstration (ἀπόδειξις) about them or proof/establishment (κατασκευή) of their having happened? Or are Herodotus and Pindar considered by you not to lie (ἀψευδεῖν), but those who practised (μελετάω) dying for the teachings (μαθήματα) of Jesus and who left (καταλείπω) to those following such writings (γράμματα) about the things of which they were persuaded (πείθω), about fictions, as you think, and myths (μῦθοι) and wonder-tales so greatly struggle (ἀγωνίζομαι) as both to live amid hardships (περιστατικῶς) on account of them and to die violently (βιαίως)? Setting yourself (ἵστημι) in the middle (μέσον) then of the things written about Aristeas and the things recorded (ἱστορέω) about Jesus, see whether from the outcome (τὸ ἀποβάν) and from those being benefited (ὠφελέω) toward correction (ἐπανόρθωσις) of characters (ἤθη) and reverence (εὐλάβεια) toward the God over all (ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός) it is not possible to say that one must believe (πιστευτέον) the things recorded about Jesus as having happened not without God (οὐκ ἀθεεί), but not those about Aristeas the Proconnesian.
pass_b_english: To the story about Aristeas we must say this. If Celsus had set it out as a story, without also showing his own assent as one who had accepted it as true, we would have met his argument in another way. But he says that Aristeas vanished in a supernatural way, appeared again plainly, visited many parts of the world and reported marvels; and he also sets out the oracle of Apollo, who enjoined the Metapontines to count Aristeas among the gods, in his own voice and with assent. So we address our reply to him: How is it that you take the marvels recorded about Jesus by his disciples to be sheer fictions, and blame those who believe them, yet do not consider these stories either tall tales or fictions? And how is it that you, who accuse others of believing the marvels about Jesus without reason, show that you have believed so many such things yourself, bringing no proof about them and no argument that they happened? Or are Herodotus and Pindar held by you to be free of falsehood, while those who trained themselves to die for the teachings of Jesus, and who left to those after them such writings about the things they were convinced of, contend so hard for what you think are fictions, myths and tall tales that for their sake they live amid hardships and die by violence?

Place yourself, then, midway between what is written about Aristeas and what is related about Jesus, and see whether, from the outcome and from those who are helped to amend their characters and to revere the God over all, it is not possible to say that we must believe the things related about Jesus, as things that did not happen without God, but not the things about Aristeas of Proconnesus.

choices.choice: Koetschau marks a crux (†) before 'λόγον τὸν πρὸς αὐτόν': the main verb is lost. The sense ('our reply to him is this') is clear from what follows, so the reading text supplies the minimum, 'So we address our reply to him'; this verb is not in the Greek. Origen restates Celsus's phrases (vanished supernaturally, appeared plainly, visited many parts of the world, reported marvels, Apollo's command) in indirect speech, so they are not placed in quotation marks. οὔ(τε) is Koetschau's supplement. τερατεία rendered 'tall tales'. 'ἀποθνῄσκειν μελετήσαντες' ('trained themselves to die') echoes Plato's description of philosophy as practising death (Phaedo 67e); an echo, not a quotation, so not cited inline. 'οὐκ ἀθεεί' rendered 'not without God'. No Scripture quoted.
removed added 'simply' in 'set it out as a story' (ὡς ἱστορίαν; the contrast is carried by the following 'without also showing his own assent')
'the oracle of Apollo, enjoining the Metapontines' -> 'the oracle of Apollo, who enjoined the Metapontines' (ἐπισκήψαντος agrees with τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος, not with χρησμόν)
'those who have been helped' -> 'those who are helped' (present participle τῶν ὠφελουμένων)
